column4: We have a part to play in the church, and while we know that we need training, we also need purification. To really be prepared for God’s purposes we must be sanctified.
column5: We are part of the church, and although we know that we need training, we also need cleansing. To be truly prepared for God's purposes we must be sanctified.

column4: The definition of **sanctification** is to purify something for a special purpose. This is closely related to the term **consecration** which means to set something aside for a special purpose.
column5: The definition of **sanctification** is to cleanse something for a specific purpose. This is closely related to the word **setting apart** which means to place something for a specific purpose.

column4: Imagine a master sculptor preparing to work with a large block of marble. The master imagines what this raw and unshaped marble can be transformed into through his careful craftsmanship. He has a very specific design in mind, he orders his assistants to set this block of marble aside for a special design (**consecration**). As he refines and works the marble, adding texture, depth, and shape, he purifies it (**sanctifies**) for that special design. The act of dedicating the marble for his special project was quick, whereas the process of shaping the marble into its final design takes considerable patience.
column5: Consider a master sculptor preparing to work on a large block of marble. The master envisions what this raw, unshaped marble can be transformed into through his careful craftsmanship. He has a very specific design in mind, and he orders his assistants to set this piece of marble in a place reserved for that specific design (**setting apart**). As he further refines and works the marble, adding surface detail, depth, and form, he purifies it (**sanctifies it**) for that specific design. The act of dedicating the marble to his special project was instantaneous, whereas the process of shaping the marble to its final design requires great patience.

column4: We were set aside, consecrated to God at salvation. Through the act of purifying our souls by the help of the Spirit we become transformed. This process of purification is what sanctifies us.
column5: When we received salvation we were set apart, and God consecrated us. As our souls are cleansed, and in cooperation with the Spirit, we are transformed. This process of cleansing is the one that sanctifies us.

column4: When we received Jesus through salvation, we were born-again. We were justified, our sins forgiven. Our spirit was regenerated, we became alive in Christ. Such a marvelous transformation that the scriptures say, “*there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” (*Luke 15:10).

column4: The word ‘carnal’ comes from the Latin root meaning ‘flesh’ or ‘meat.’ The carnal nature is inside of each of us from birth, like an animal’s instincts, it exists to help us survive. The way the carnal nature works is by being self-focused, self-oriented, self-centered. Children are natural examples of a fleshly nature. Despite their innocence, their nature is focused primarily on their wants, desires, needs; and ‘watch out!’ if you don’t meet its every expectation.

column4: Pruning is incredibly healthy for a plant. Thinking back to our chapter on repentance, we are called to turn away from dead works (those works that are no longer bearing fruit) and turn toward God. The result of this turning away from the dead places in our life, and towards God, empowers the great gardener of our life to prune branches, improve growth, and produce greater spiritual fruit (John 15:2).
column5: Pruning is very healthy for a plant. Returning to our chapter on repentance, we are called to turn away from dead works (which are works that no longer bear fruit) and to turn to God. The result of turning away from the dead places in our lives, and turning to God, enables the great vinedresser of our lives to prune the branches, improve growth, and produce even more spiritual fruit (John 15:2).

column4: While pruning can feel painful, it reflects God’s loving care as He shapes us into vessels for His purpose (Hebrews 12:11). Some may feel a sense of loss, even fear, when undergoing the pruning process. However, God is gentle, and even a bruised reed He will not break (Isaiah 42:3). Grapevines are pruned during their dormant season to minimize stress on the plant. The gardener tending the growth will cut back old and woody growth that no longer produces fruit like it used to, this allows the vine to direct energy into the branches with the most potential for good fruit.
column5: Although pruning may seem painful, it nevertheless demonstrates the loving care of God as He makes us into vessels for His purpose (Hebrews 12:11). Some may feel loss, even fear, as they go through the process of pruning. However, God is merciful; He will not break even a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3). Grapevines are pruned during their dormant season to reduce stress on the plant. The vinedresser who tends the growth cuts away the aged, woody growth that no longer bears fruit as before; this allows the vine to direct energy to the branches most likely to produce good fruit.

column4: Like a gardener trimming branches to direct growth, God may allow seasons of correction and discipline to refine our faith and character, but His work is patient and kind. God prunes those who abide in him. Our focus is to be more on the abiding in Christ, and less on the work of the pruning.

God prunes those who abide in Him. Our focus should be more on abiding in Christ and less on the work of pruning.

column4: #### **1. Explicit Memory (Declarative Memory)**
column5: #### **1. Explicit Memory (Declarative Memory)**

column4: **Purpose:** Stores facts, events, and experiences that we can consciously recall. It’s split into two types-**semantic** and **episodic** memory.
column5: **Purpose:** It stores facts, events, and experiences we can consciously recall. It is divided into two types-**semantic** and **episodic** memory.

column4: **Semantic Memory - Facts and Knowledge.** Semantic memory is where we store facts, definitions, and general knowledge-things like historical dates, Bible verses, and practical information. It helps us predict outcomes, make decisions, and avoid danger (e.g., recognizing poisonous plants). While it gives us stability and order, it can also lead to rigidity-an over-reliance on rules rather than adapting to unexpected situations.

column4: **Episodic Memory - Personal Experiences.** Episodic memory stores our personal experiences, tying them to specific times and places-like a wedding day or a traumatic event. These memories provide context, helping us learn from the past and build relationships. However, episodic memory is prone to emotional bias and distortion. Past trauma can create fearful associations, making it difficult to move forward.

column4: Renewing the mind isn’t a quick fix-it’s a process of gradual transformation that is lifelong. Each memory system plays a role in shaping how we think, feel, and act. By intentionally working with the Holy Spirit, applying Scripture, and developing godly habits, we can train our minds to align with God’s truth. Whether addressing past wounds, learning new habits, or staying focused in the moment, God has provided both **spiritual tools** and **practical wisdom** to help us walk in renewal and freedom (2 Corinthians 10:5).
column5: Mental renewal is not a quick fix—it is a gradual, lifelong process of change. Each of the memory systems plays a role in shaping how we think, feel, and act. By intentionally working with the Holy Spirit, applying Scripture, and developing God-honoring habits, we can train our minds to align with God's truth. Whether we are dealing with past wounds, learning new habits, or focusing on the moment, God has provided both **spiritual tools** and **practical wisdom** to help us walk in renewal and freedom (2 Corinthians 10:5).

column4: Our world is full of trouble, tribulation, and trial. Through the disciplined renewing of the mind, our souls become transformed, and we can live a life of freedom unto God full of the fruit of His Spirit (Galatians 5:22-25).
column5: Our world is full of trouble, suffering, and trials. By renewing the mind with discipline, our souls are transformed, and we can live a life of freedom for God, full of the fruit of His Spirit (Galatians 5:22-25).
